pos: n. (a rounded compass; the vault or round of the earth)
etymology: From the Latin circulus, a ring. The Hebrew chug means a circuit or vault. It stands once in the KJV text proper, in Isaiah's picture of God enthroned above the round of the earth.
biblical_def: Isaiah is arguing against despair, and his argument is a place: “It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in” (Isaiah 40:22). The circle is the vault or compass of the earth, and the point of the sentence is the vantage: God is seated above it, and from that seat the nations are what a grasshopper is to a man. The chapter presses the comparison further: “Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing” (Isaiah 40:15). Princes are handled the same way: “That bringeth the princes to nothing; he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity” (Isaiah 40:23). And the whole meditation exists for the sake of a discouraged people, which is why it ends where it does: “But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). Isaiah does not comfort exiles by making their trouble smaller. He comforts them by showing them where God sits.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines circle as a plane figure comprehended by a single curve line called its circumference; a round body; an orb.
webster_full: CIRCLE, n. In geometry, a plane figure comprehended by a single curve line called its circumference; a round body; an orb.
COMPASS, n. A circle; a circuit; the extent or limit of ground within a circle.
CURTAIN, n. A cloth hanging round a bed or at a window, which may be contracted, spread or drawn aside at pleasure.
CANOPY, n. A covering over a throne or over a bed; a covering spread over the head.
SOVEREIGN, a. Supreme in power; possessing supreme dominion; superior to all others.
scriptures: Isaiah 40:22
It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in:
Isaiah 40:15
Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing.
Isaiah 40:23
That bringeth the princes to nothing; he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity.
Isaiah 40:31
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
corruption_summary: The verse is pressed into service as a scientific proof text about the shape of the earth, which trades a doctrine of God's transcendence for an argument Isaiah was not making.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 40:22 is widely quoted as evidence that Scripture anticipated modern cosmology by describing a spherical earth. The apologetic is well meant and it misplaces the weight of the sentence. The Hebrew word means a circuit or vault, the clause that follows compares the heavens to a tent, and the whole verse is built to establish where God sits rather than what shape the earth is. Making the text a scientific claim invites the reader to judge Scripture by whether it scored a point, when the passage is asking him to consider the One seated above the circuit and the grasshoppers below it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is that biblical comfort works by enlarging the view of God rather than by minimising the trouble. Chapter 40 opens with Comfort ye, comfort ye my people and then spends twenty verses on God's incomparability — the nations a drop in a bucket, the princes brought to nothing, the stars called out by name. Only then does it reach the promise about renewed strength. That order is deliberate and it is pastoral: a discouraged saint does not need his difficulty explained away; he needs to be told again who sits upon the circle of the earth.
roots_summary: Hebrew chug (H2329), a circle or vault; arets (H776), the earth; dallah (H1803), a drop; qavah (H6960), to wait or hope.
roots_lines: Hebrew chug (H2329) — a circuit, vault, compass; the circle of the earth, Isaiah 40:22.
Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to sit, be enthroned; it is he that sitteth upon it.
Hebrew chagab (H2284) — a grasshopper; what the inhabitants are from that seat.
Hebrew ayin (H369) — nothing, nought; the princes brought to nothing.
Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, look for; they that wait upon the LORD.
usage: “He that sitteth upon the circle of the earth” — the vantage of the throne.
“The nations are as a drop of a bucket” — the scale that follows from it.
“They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength” — where the comfort lands.

pos: adj. (full of people; numerous in inhabitants)
etymology: From the Latin populosus, from populus, a people. Scripture uses it twice: of what Israel became in Egypt, and of a great Egyptian city that fell anyway.
biblical_def: The confession an Israelite made when he brought his firstfruits begins with a wanderer and ends with a nation: “And thou shalt speak and say before the LORD thy God, A Syrian ready to perish was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there with a few, and became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous” (Deuteronomy 26:5). The worshipper rehearses his own smallness before he presents his basket. The multiplication he describes was promised long before: “And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing” (Genesis 12:2). The other use turns the same word into a warning. Nahum asks Nineveh to look at a city that had everything she has: “Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?” (Nahum 3:8). No — Thebes — was populous, moated, walled and defended, and it fell. Numbers are a blessing when God gives them and no defence when He does not: “There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength” (Psalm 33:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines populous as full of inhabitants; containing many inhabitants in proportion to the extent of the country.
webster_full: POPULOUS, a. Full of inhabitants; containing many inhabitants in proportion to the extent of the country.
POPULATION, n. The whole number of people in a country, province, city or district.
MULTITUDE, n. The state of being many; a great number, collectively.
RAMPART, n. In fortification, an elevation or mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting the cannon of an enemy.
SOJOURN, v.i. To dwell for a time; to dwell or live in a place as a temporary resident.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 26:5

And thou shalt speak and say before the LORD thy God, A Syrian ready to perish was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there with a few, and became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous:
Genesis 12:2
And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing:
Nahum 3:8
Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?
Psalm 33:16
There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength.
corruption_summary: Numbers are treated as the measure of a work's validity, which is precisely the confidence Nahum dismantles and the Psalms deny.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Scripture's double verdict on multitude. Israel's growth into a populous nation was a covenant blessing, explicitly promised to Abraham and explicitly confessed at the altar — so numbers are not despised. And populous No, with a river for a moat and the sea for a wall, was destroyed — so numbers are not trusted. The two statements sit in the same canon without tension because both are about who gives increase and who withholds deliverance.

The live misuse in the church is the use of attendance as the proof of faithfulness. It works in both directions and is wrong in both. A large congregation is taken as divine endorsement, and a small one as evidence of failure or of superior purity. Neither inference has any scriptural warrant. Gideon's army was reduced by God on purpose so that Israel could not vaunt itself; the crowd that followed our Lord for the loaves thinned to twelve when He preached hard words; and three thousand were added in a day at Pentecost. The confession an Israelite made over his basket keeps the right order: a perishing Syrian was my father, and God made him a nation.
roots_summary: Hebrew rab (H7227), many, numerous; goy gadol, a great nation; atsum (H6099), mighty; hamon (H1995), a multitude.
roots_lines: Hebrew rab (H7227) — many, great, populous; Deuteronomy 26:5.
Hebrew atsum (H6099) — mighty, numerous; great, mighty, and populous.
Hebrew goy (H1471) — a nation; what the sojourning few became.
Hebrew amon (H528) — populous, of the multitude; Nahum 3:8 of No.
Hebrew hamon (H1995) — a multitude, host; Psalm 33:16, no king saved by it.
usage: “Became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous” — the firstfruits confession.
“Art thou better than populous No?” — a great city that fell.
“No king saved by the multitude of an host” — what numbers cannot do.

pos: adj. and n. (firmly established; also a shelter for beasts)
etymology: From the Latin stabilis, firm, from stare, to stand. The two occurrences hold both senses — the world made stable by God's hand, and a ruined capital turned into a stable for camels.
biblical_def: David's psalm at the bringing up of the ark grounds the world's steadiness in God: “Fear before him, all the earth: the world also shall be stable, that it be not moved” (1 Chronicles 16:30). The stability is not a property the creation holds on its own; it follows a command to fear, and it belongs to the God being praised. The second use is judgment in the other sense of the word: “And I will make Rabbah a stable for camels, and the Ammonites a couchingplace for flocks: and ye shall know that I am the LORD” (Ezekiel 25:5). A capital city becomes a shed. What God establishes stands and what He overturns becomes pasture, and the same divine name is given as the reason in both cases. The Psalter says the same thing of the throne: “Thy throne is established of old: thou art from everlasting” (Psalm 93:2). And the New Testament applies the distinction to everything that can be shaken: “And this word, Yet once more, signifieth the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain” (Hebrews 12:27). Stability in Scripture is never intrinsic. It is conferred, and it is conferred on what God has chosen to keep.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stable as fixed; firmly established; not to be easily moved or overthrown; and as a house or shed for beasts.
webster_full: STABLE, a. Fixed; firmly established; not to be easily moved, shaken or overthrown.
STABLE, n. A house or shed for beasts to lodge and feed in; a building for horses or cattle.
ESTABLISH, v.t. To set and fix firmly or unalterably; to settle permanently.
COUCHING-PLACE, n. A place where beasts lie down to rest; a resting place for flocks.
IMMUTABLE, a. Unchangeable; not capable or susceptible of change.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 16:30
Fear before him, all the earth: the world also shall be stable, that it be not moved.
Ezekiel 25:5
And I will make Rabbah a stable for camels, and the Ammonites a couchingplace for flocks: and ye shall know that I am the LORD.
Psalm 93:2
Thy throne is established of old: thou art from everlasting.
Hebrews 12:27
And this word, Yet once more, signifieth the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain.
corruption_summary: Stability is sought in what is made rather than in the One who makes, and the created order is treated as self-sustaining rather than upheld.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of providence as continuous upholding. A deistic instinct — common among people who would never name it — imagines the world as a mechanism wound up and left running, stable because of how it was built. Scripture describes it otherwise: the world is stable because He upholds all things by the word of His power, and by Him all things consist. The steadiness of the ground underfoot is an act, not a property, and the Chronicler's psalm puts the command to fear God in the same breath as the promise that the world shall not be moved.

Ezekiel's use is the sobering half. Rabbah was a capital, and God made it a stable for camels. Nothing built by men is stable in the first sense merely because it has stood a long time, and Hebrews says plainly that everything shakeable will be shaken precisely so that what cannot be shaken may remain. That is a promise before it is a threat: the believer's security does not rest on any arrangement he can see. It rests on a kingdom which cannot be moved, received rather than constructed.
roots_summary: Hebrew kun (H3559), to be firmly established; mot (H4131), to be moved or shaken; naveh (H5116), a habitation or pasture; Greek saleuo (G4531), to shake.
roots_lines: Hebrew kun (H3559) — to be established, made firm; the world shall be stable.
Hebrew mot (H4131) — to totter, be moved; that it be not moved.
Hebrew naveh (H5116) — a pasture, dwelling of flocks; Rabbah made a stable.
Hebrew olam (H5769) — everlasting, of old; thy throne is established of old.
Greek saleuo (G4531) — to shake, agitate; the removing of things that are shaken.
usage: “The world also shall be stable, that it be not moved” — steadiness conferred by God.
“I will make Rabbah a stable for camels” — a capital reduced to pasture.
“Those things which cannot be shaken may remain” — the final sifting.

pos: n. (a prosperous outcome; the favourable issue of an undertaking)
etymology: From the Latin successus, an advance or good result. The word stands once in the KJV, in the charge given to Joshua at the Jordan, and it is tied there to a book rather than to a battle plan.
biblical_def: God commissions Joshua for a conquest and gives him one instrument: “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success” (Joshua 1:8). The chain is exact — the book in the mouth, meditation day and night, observance of what is written, and then prosperity and good success. Nothing is said about strategy or numbers. The command is repeated with its condition twice over: “Only be thou strong and very courageous, that thou mayest observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded thee: turn not from it to the right hand or to the left, that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest” (Joshua 1:7). The same doctrine opens the Psalter: “But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psalm 1:2), with its result, “And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper” (Psalm 1:3). Success in Scripture is the fruit of obedience to a revealed word, not an outcome pursued directly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines success as the favorable or prosperous termination of anything attempted; and good success as a prosperous issue.
webster_full: SUCCESS, n. The favorable or prosperous termination of anything attempted; a termination which answers the purpose intended.
PROSPER, v.i. To be successful; to succeed; to be advanced in the pursuit of anything desirable.
MEDITATE, v.i. To dwell on anything in thought; to contemplate; to revolve in the mind.
LAW, n. In Scripture, the Mosaic institutions, or the revealed will of God; the rule of moral conduct.
OBSERVE, v.t. To keep religiously; to celebrate; to obey; to follow.
scriptures: Joshua 1:8

This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.
Joshua 1:7

Only be thou strong and very courageous, that thou mayest observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded thee: turn not from it to the right hand or to the left, that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest.
Psalm 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
Psalm 1:3
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
corruption_summary: Joshua 1:8 is detached from its object and used as a promise of career and financial advancement, so that a command about obeying a book becomes a technique for getting results.
corruption_paragraphs: No verse in the Old Testament is more regularly stripped of its terms than this one. The promise of good success is quoted, the conditions are dropped, and the whole is offered as an assurance that God will prosper the believer's plans. The verse says the opposite of what that use requires. The success promised is contingent on meditating in the law day and night and on observing to do all that is written therein, and the undertaking in view is the possession of Canaan under a divine mandate. A man may meet none of those conditions and quote the verse over a business.

The deeper corruption is in the definition of success itself. Prosperity teaching measures it by health, income and influence; Scripture measures it by whether a man did what God commanded. By the world's standard Jeremiah failed for forty years, our Lord failed at Calvary, and Stephen failed under the stones. Hebrews 11 lists men who subdued kingdoms and men who were sawn asunder in the same breath and calls both faith. The Reformed instinct here is the Westminster answer applied to vocation: the chief end is to glorify God and enjoy Him for ever, and any success that costs that end is failure with a good outcome attached.
roots_summary: Hebrew sakal (H7919), to act wisely and so prosper; tsalach (H6743), to advance, prosper; hagah (H1897), to meditate, mutter; torah (H8451), law, instruction.

Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to advance, prosper; make thy way prosperous.
Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to mutter, meditate; the day-and-night occupation with the book.
Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, direction; what must not depart out of the mouth.

“Turn not from it to the right hand or to the left” — the terms repeated.
“Whatsoever he doeth shall prosper” — the Psalter's parallel.

etymology: From the Latin unitus, made one. The word occurs once, in Jacob's deathbed oracle over Simeon and Levi, where a dying father refuses to let his own honour be joined to his sons' assembly.
biblical_def: Jacob blesses his sons and comes to two he cannot bless: “O my soul, come not thou into their secret; unto their assembly, mine honour, be not thou united: for in their anger they slew a man, and in their selfwill they digged down a wall” (Genesis 49:6). The reference is to Shechem, where Simeon and Levi avenged their sister by slaughter under the cover of a covenant sign. Jacob names the offence and then curses the thing rather than the men: “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7). The refusal to be united is a refusal of complicity, and Scripture asks the same separation of every believer: “Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful” (Psalm 1:1). Paul states it as a command with the covenant promise attached: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6:14). The dying patriarch's instinct is the scriptural one: there are assemblies a man's honour must not enter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unite as to put together or join two or more things, which make one mass or compound; and united as made one; joined.
webster_full: UNITE, v.t. To put together or join two or more things, which make one mass or compound; to make one.
UNITED, pp. Made one; joined; cemented; made to agree.
CONFEDERACY, n. A league or covenant; a contract between two or more persons or states.
COMPLICITY, n. The state of being an accomplice; participation in guilt.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company of persons collected together in one place, usually for some common purpose.
scriptures: Genesis 49:6
O my soul, come not thou into their secret; unto their assembly, mine honour, be not thou united: for in their anger they slew a man, and in their selfwill they digged down a wall.
Genesis 49:7
Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.
Psalm 1:1
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
2 Corinthians 6:14
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
corruption_summary: Unity is elevated into an unqualified good, so that separation on grounds of righteousness is treated as the sin and partnership in wrong as maturity.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reflex treats unity as self-evidently virtuous and division as self-evidently sinful, and on that reflex Jacob's words are unintelligible. Scripture's position is that unity is good when it is unity in the truth and is a sin when it is confederacy in wrong. Isaiah was told not to say a confederacy to all them to whom this people shall say a confederacy; Paul commanded the Corinthians not to be unequally yoked; our Lord said He came to bring a sword into households. The question Scripture asks of any union is never whether it is a union but what it is a union in.

The ecumenical application follows directly. A unity purchased by agreeing not to settle what justification is, or what the gospel is, is the assembly Jacob would not let his honour enter. The Reformation did not divide the church for preference; it divided over whether a man is justified by faith alone, and the confessions that came out of it treat that as a matter on which unity is impossible without agreement. At the same time Scripture's rebuke of needless division is just as sharp — Paul on the Corinthian parties, our Lord praying that they all may be one. The discipline is to hold both, and it requires knowing which questions are which.

pos: n. (a hazard; chance — in the phrase at a venture, at random)
etymology: A contraction of adventure, from the Latin adventurus, about to happen. In both occurrences it describes an archer shooting without aim, and in both it kills a king God had already sentenced.
biblical_def: Ahab had gone to Ramoth-gilead in disguise, having been warned by Micaiah that he would not return, and the arrow found him anyway: “And a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness: wherefore he said unto the driver of his chariot, Turn thine hand, and carry me out of the host; for I am wounded” (1 Kings 22:34). The Chronicler records it in almost identical words, as though the detail were too important to paraphrase: “And a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness” (2 Chronicles 18:33). Two things are true at once. The archer aimed at nobody; and the arrow went through the one seam in the armour of the one man in the field who had been told he would die there. The prophet's word had been plain: “And Micaiah said, If thou return at all in peace, the LORD hath not spoken by me. And he said, Hearken, O people, every one of you” (1 Kings 22:28). Solomon states the principle the chapter illustrates: “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines venture as a hazard; an undertaking of chance or danger; and at a venture, at hazard, without seeing the end or mark.
webster_full: VENTURE, n. A hazard; an undertaking of chance or danger; the risking of something upon an event.
AT A VENTURE, at hazard; without seeing the end or mark, or without foreseeing the issue.
HARNESS, n. Armor; the furniture of a military man; the accoutrements of a horse.
LOT, n. That which, in human speech, is called chance, hazard, fortune; but in strictness of language, is the determination of Providence.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: 1 Kings 22:34

And a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness: wherefore he said unto the driver of his chariot, Turn thine hand, and carry me out of the host; for I am wounded.
2 Chronicles 18:33

And a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness: therefore he said to his chariot man, Turn thine hand, that thou mayest carry me out of the host; for I am wounded.
1 Kings 22:28
And Micaiah said, If thou return at all in peace, the LORD hath not spoken by me. And he said, Hearken, O people, every one of you.
Proverbs 16:33
The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
corruption_summary: The account is read as coincidence dressed up as prophecy, or else providence is defended in a way that makes the archer a puppet rather than a man who drew his own bow.
corruption_paragraphs: The sceptical reading is straightforward: a random arrow killed a king, and the narrator afterwards attached a prophecy to it. The text forecloses that move by reporting the prophecy first, in public, with Micaiah staking his standing as a prophet on the outcome and being imprisoned for saying it. Ahab believed the warning enough to disguise himself, which is why the chapter is such a precise study — every human precaution was taken, the archer had no target, and the sentence was executed exactly.

The opposite error over-corrects. In defending God's sovereignty some speak as though the archer were moved like a piece on a board, his will suspended, his act not truly his. The confessions are careful here in a way that popular teaching often is not. God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, and yet no violence is offered to the will of the creature, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away but rather established. The man drew his bow at a venture; the arrow went where God appointed. Both sentences are true, and Scripture states them side by side without apology.

Hebrew qesheth (H7198) — a bow; drawn by a man with no target.
Hebrew debeq (H1694) — a joint, seam; between the joints of the harness.
Hebrew goral (H1486) — a lot; cast into the lap, disposed by the LORD.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment; the sentence Micaiah announced.

“Between the joints of the harness” — the one seam in the armour.
“The whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” — the doctrine in a proverb.

pos: v. (to chirp or squeak faintly, as a bird or a spirit-voice)
etymology: Imitative, of the thin cry of a young bird. Isaiah uses it with contempt of the noises made by mediums — a chirping from the ground rather than a word from heaven.
biblical_def: Isaiah reports what Judah was being urged to do and answers it with a question: “And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” (Isaiah 8:19). The verbs are chosen to belittle. A wizard does not speak; he peeps and mutters, making the thin chirping of a bird from a hole in the ground. The prophet then gives the test by which every such voice is to be judged: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isaiah 8:20). The law forbade the whole traffic without exception: “Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer” (Deuteronomy 18:11). And Isaiah turns the same chirping voice into a picture of Jerusalem humbled: “And thou shalt be brought down, and shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be, as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust” (Isaiah 29:4). A people who consult the dead end by sounding like them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines peep as to cry, as chickens; to utter a fine shrill sound, as a small bird or a mouse.
webster_full: PEEP, v.i. To cry, as chickens; to utter a fine shrill sound, as a small bird or a mouse.
MUTTER, v.i. To utter words with a low voice and compressed lips, with sullenness or in complaint; to grumble.
WIZARD, n. A conjurer; an enchanter; a sorcerer; one who practices the black art.
FAMILIAR SPIRIT, a demon or evil spirit supposed to attend at call; one consulted by necromancers.
NECROMANCY, n. The art of revealing future events by means of a pretended communication with the dead.
scriptures: Isaiah 8:19
And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?
Isaiah 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Deuteronomy 18:11
Or a charmer , or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer .
Isaiah 29:4

And thou shalt be brought down, and shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be, as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust.
corruption_summary: Divination is rebranded as spirituality, wellness or intuition, and a practice Scripture puts under the death penalty is retailed as harmless self-discovery.
corruption_paragraphs: The vocabulary has changed and the traffic has not. What Deuteronomy calls consulting familiar spirits now circulates as channelling, mediumship, tarot, astrology, crystals, manifesting and contacting the ancestors — sold as self-knowledge and marketed hardest to the bereaved and the anxious. Scripture's judgment does not depend on whether the practitioner is sincere or whether anything happens. It is an abomination unto the LORD because it seeks from the dead what God has given in His word, and because behind the theatre there is a real adversary who does not advertise himself.

Isaiah supplies the church's test in a single clause: to the law and to the testimony. Any voice claiming to speak for God — a medium, a dream, an impression, a modern prophet, an angel — is measured against what is written, and a voice that does not speak according to this word has no light in it. That principle is the ground of the Reformed doctrine of the sufficiency and finality of Scripture, and it is why the dictionary is cessationist: the canon is closed, God has spoken in His Son, and a people who have the law and the testimony have no business at the mouth of a hole in the ground.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaphaph (H6850), to chirp or peep; hagah (H1897), to mutter; ob (H178), a familiar spirit; yiddeoni (H3049), a wizard.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaphaph (H6850) — to chirp, peep as a bird; Isaiah 8:19 of the wizards.

Hebrew ob (H178) — a familiar spirit, or the medium who has one.
Hebrew yiddeoni (H3049) — a knowing one, a wizard; from the root to know.
Hebrew torah and teudah (H8451, H8584) — the law and the testimony, Isaiah 8:20.
usage: “Wizards that peep, and that mutter” — Isaiah's contempt for the medium's voice.
“Should not a people seek unto their God?” — the question that answers the practice.
“To the law and to the testimony” — the test for every claimed voice.

pos: adv. (to a great depth; profoundly; thoroughly)
etymology: From deep, Saxon deop. Scripture uses the adverb to intensify three things: revolt, corruption, and the sighing of the Son of God.
biblical_def: Isaiah measures a nation's apostasy by the word: “Turn ye unto him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted” (Isaiah 31:6). The revolt is not a drift but a descent, and the call to turn is addressed to men who have gone a long way down. Hosea uses the same adverb of a moral condition: “They have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah: therefore he will remember their iniquity, he will visit their sins” (Hosea 9:9). The reference to Gibeah points back to the worst chapter in Judges, and the point is that the corruption has reached that depth again. Then Mark applies the word to the Lord Jesus: “And he sighed deeply in his spirit, and saith, Why doth this generation seek after a sign? verily I say unto you, There shall no sign be given unto this generation” (Mark 8:12). The Pharisees had asked for a sign from heaven, and the response of the incarnate Son is a groan that comes from His spirit. He is not irritated; He is grieved, and the same Gospel records Him looking round on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts. The word that measures Israel's revolt is the word that measures His sorrow over it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deeply as at or to a great depth; profoundly; thoroughly; with great emotion or grief.
webster_full: DEEPLY, adv. At or to a great depth; far below the surface; profoundly.
DEEPLY, adv. With great emotion; sorrowfully; with deep affection or grief.
REVOLT, v.i. To fall off or turn from one to another; to renounce allegiance and subjection.
CORRUPT, v.t. To become putrid; to lose purity; to be vitiated; to be depraved.
SIGH, v.i. To draw in a long breath and expel it audibly, as the effect of grief or oppression.
scriptures: Isaiah 31:6
Turn ye unto him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted.
Hosea 9:9
They have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah: therefore he will remember their iniquity, he will visit their sins.
Mark 8:12
And he sighed deeply in his spirit, and saith, Why doth this generation seek after a sign? verily I say unto you, There shall no sign be given unto this generation.
Mark 3:5

And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.
corruption_summary: The affections of Christ are flattened by a sentimentality that makes Him only gentle, or by a false doctrine of impassibility that leaves the incarnate Son unable to grieve.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 8:12 is a hard verse for two opposite instincts. The first is the popular sentimentality that knows only a mild and endlessly accommodating Jesus; it has no category for a Saviour who groans at a request and refuses it flatly. The second is a careless handling of divine impassibility that, in guarding God against change, leaves no room for the real human sorrow of the Man of sorrows. The Chalcedonian confession the dictionary holds keeps both: one Person in two natures, without confusion and without division. The divine nature does not suffer alteration; the Son of God truly sighed in His spirit, truly wept at a grave, and truly was grieved at the hardness of men's hearts.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the seriousness of degrees in sin. Isaiah says Israel had deeply revolted and Hosea that they had deeply corrupted themselves, which means Scripture reckons that sin can go further down — that a conscience can be seared, a heart hardened, a nation brought to Gibeah again. Against a flat view in which all sin is simply sin, the prophets insist on descent, and against despair they attach to the deepest word in Isaiah's sentence a command: turn ye unto him. There is no depth from which that call does not reach.

usage: “The children of Israel have deeply revolted” — apostasy measured as descent.
“They have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah” — the depth named.
“He sighed deeply in his spirit” — the grief of the incarnate Son.

pos: adv. (splendidly; with showy magnificence of dress)
etymology: From gorgeous, Old French gorgias, showy. Both occurrences concern clothing that impresses — the Assyrian captains Oholibah doted on, and the soft raiment our Lord says is found in kings' courts and not in the wilderness.
biblical_def: Ezekiel describes a nation seduced by the look of power: “She doted upon the Assyrians her neighbours, captains and rulers clothed most gorgeously, horsemen riding upon horses, all of them desirable young men” (Ezekiel 23:12). The uniform does the work; the alliance follows the impression. Our Lord uses the word while correcting a crowd's expectations about John the Baptist: “But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? Behold, they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts” (Luke 7:25). The wilderness prophet was not dressed for a court, and the crowd had gone out to hear a man whose clothing announced that he had nothing to protect. Christ's verdict on him follows immediately: “But what went ye out for to see? A prophet? Yea, I say unto you, and much more than a prophet” (Luke 7:26). Peter draws the apostolic conclusion for Christian women, and in doing so for all believers: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; but let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price” (1 Peter 3:3-4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gorgeous as showy; fine; splendid; and gorgeously as with showy magnificence; splendidly.
webster_full: GORGEOUS, a. Showy; fine; splendid; glittering with gay colors; magnificent.
GORGEOUSLY, adv. With showy magnificence; splendidly; finely.
APPAREL, n. Clothing; vesture; garments; dress; external habiliments.
DELICATELY, adv. In a delicate manner; luxuriously; with nice regard to ease and softness.
ADORNING, n. Ornament; decoration; that which embellishes.
scriptures: Ezekiel 23:12
She doted upon the Assyrians her neighbours, captains and rulers clothed most gorgeously, horsemen riding upon horses, all of them desirable young men.
Luke 7:25
But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? Behold, they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts.
Luke 7:26
But what went ye out for to see? A prophet? Yea, I say unto you, and much more than a prophet.
1 Peter 3:4
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: Display is defended as self-expression and judged only by whether it offends, while Scripture asks a different question — what the appearance is for, and whom it is meant to impress.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture is interested in the purpose of appearance rather than in a list of forbidden fabrics. Ezekiel's indictment is not that Assyrian officers dressed well; it is that Oholibah doted on them because they did, and made a ruinous alliance on the strength of an impression. Our Lord's remark is not that soft raiment is sinful; it is that a prophet does not wear it, and the crowd had gone to the wilderness for a prophet. The question in both places is what the clothing is doing.

Two errors follow when that question is lost. One is an external legalism that measures holiness by plainness and produces its own kind of display, which is the older Puritan temptation honestly named. The other, far more common now, treats appearance as a sphere of pure self-expression exempt from Christian reflection altogether. Peter's instruction cuts between them. He does not forbid clothing or hair; he says let it not be that outward adorning, and directs the labour of self-presentation to the hidden man of the heart. The standard given is what is of great price in the sight of God, which is a different audience than the one gorgeous apparel is aimed at.

“They which are gorgeously apparelled…are in kings' courts” — not in the wilderness.
“The ornament of a meek and quiet spirit” — the adorning of great price.

pos: adj. (resembling a lion in strength or ferocity)
etymology: A compound formed to render a Hebrew word meaning lion-like or heroic. It occurs twice, both times of two men of Moab slain by Benaiah, one of David's mighty men.
biblical_def: Benaiah's record is given in one dense sentence: “And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man, of Kabzeel, who had done many acts, he slew two lionlike men of Moab: he went down also and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow” (2 Samuel 23:20). The Chronicler repeats it almost word for word: “Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts; he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day” (1 Chronicles 11:22). The description is deliberate in its order — two men called lionlike, then an actual lion, in a pit, in snow, and he went down to it. The next verse adds the Egyptian with a spear whom Benaiah met with a staff. Scripture keeps such lists because it honours courage exercised in the service of God's anointed, and it keeps them without flattery: the same Benaiah later executes Joab and Shimei at Solomon's word. Against every human lion the Psalter sets the one true refuge: “Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet” (Psalm 91:13). And Peter names the lion no mighty man can kill: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lion as a quadruped of great strength and courage, and lionlike as resembling a lion in form or qualities.
webster_full: LION, n. A quadruped of the genus Felis, very strong, fierce and rapacious; the largest is eight or nine feet in length.
LION-LIKE, a. Like a lion; fierce; bold; resembling a lion in courage or strength.
VALIANT, a. Brave; courageous; intrepid in danger; heroic.
MIGHTY, a. Having great bodily strength or physical power; very strong; valiant; bold.
CHAMPION, n. A man who undertakes a combat in the place or cause of another; a hero.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 23:20

And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man , of Kabzeel, who had done many acts, he slew two lionlike men of Moab: he went down also and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow:
1 Chronicles 11:22
Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts; he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day.
Psalm 91:13
Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet.
1 Peter 5:8
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
corruption_summary: Courage is either dismissed as a merely worldly virtue or detached from its object, so that boldness is admired for its own sake rather than for what it is spent on.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture honours courage and names the men who had it. The roll of David's mighty men is not an intrusion into a spiritual book; it is a record kept deliberately, with the acts specified and the men named, because bravery spent in the service of God's anointed king is worth remembering. A piety that finds such lists embarrassing has a narrower view of virtue than the Bible does.

The opposite distortion detaches the courage from its object. Benaiah is not commended for being fierce; he is in this list because his fierceness served David. The two lionlike men of Moab were presumably brave too, and they are remembered only as men Benaiah killed. Scripture's consistent judgment is that valour takes its moral character from the cause it serves, which is why the New Testament redirects the vocabulary of warfare to a different field entirely — the whole armour of God, the good fight of faith, an adversary who is himself a roaring lion and whom no mighty man has ever killed. That lion is crushed by the Lion of the tribe of Judah, and by no one else.

Hebrew ari (H738) — a lion; the beast in the pit in time of snow.
Hebrew gibbor (H1368) — a mighty man, warrior; the class Benaiah belonged to.

“Slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow” — the detail Scripture keeps.
